To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in NIDDM patients failing to glyburide treatment, the addition of either bed time NPH or metformin treatment, improves fasting and post-prandial glucose levels, with no change in body weight and lipid levels.
the addition of either low-dose NPH insulin or metformin to the previously ineffective glyburide therapy improves glycaemic control in NIDDM patients.

in patients with secondary failure of glyburide treatment the addition of either bed-time NPH-insulin injection (0.3 U/kg) or metformin treatment (500 mg x3) significantly improves glycaemic control, with no significant difference between the two treatments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the comparison of two combined therapies in NIDDM patients who had failed to respond adequately to sulfonylureas alone.
the evaluation of the efficacy of the addition of met-formin and bed-time NPH injection to the previously ineffective glyburide treatment.
the treatment of secondary failure to glybureide in type II diabetic patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the addition of either bed-time NPH or metformin to a previously ineffective sulfonyurea treatment in secondary NIDDM failure is effective in improving glycemic control and is associated with a different metabolic profile.
the two combined therapies are similarly effective in the treatment of NIDDM, but that the addition of bed-time insulin injection causes a significant increase in the average body weight.

the addition of either bed-time NPH injection or metformin administration to the previously ineffective treatment with glyburide is an effective treatment option for NIDDM patients in secondary failure to glyburea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in NIDDM patients failing on glyburide therapy, the addition of either bed-time NPH injection or metformin treatment is effective in lowering both fasting and postprandial plasma glucose.

in NIDDM patients who fail to respond to sulfonylureas the addition of either bed-time insulin or metformin to the previous ineffective sulfonylura therapy is effective, although bed-time NPH injection seems more effective in reducing fasting plasma glucose levels and metformin seems more effective in improving post-prandial glucose levels.

the addition of either a single, bed-time NPH injection or oral metformin to the previously ineffective glyburide treatment is equally effective in improving glycemic control in NIDDM patients who are secondary failures to sulfonylureas, although the two combined therapies have different effects on fasting plasma glucose and body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of either bed-time NPH or metformin administration is effective in improving glycaemic control of patients with secondary failure of sulfonylureas.
the combination of metformin with sulfonylureas is a valid alternative to insulin treatment, especially in patients who are unwilling or unable to perform multiple daily injections.

the addition of either a single, bed time NPH-insulin injection (0.20 U/kg) or an oral administration of metformin (500 mg x3) to the sulfonylureas treatment of NIDDM-patients with secondary failure to the sulfonylaureas treatment, improves significantly the glycemic control.
